description:
¡Hola! Somos un equipo apasionado por la tecnología, el diseño y la divulgación científica, creadores de "Misión Rescate: Espejo Marciano", un juego web educativo ambientado en Marteque utiliza datos reales de la NASA (POWER y DONKI).

Buscamos entusiastas con talento en Frontend (React/TypeScript), diseño UI/UX o creatividad narrativa para pulir nuestra demo interactiva de supervivencia espacial infantil. ¡Únete para construir ciencia divertida y competir rumbo a la final global! 🚀
summary:
What is it?: It is an educational adventure and survival web game for children ages 8 to 13. The player chooses a city in Bolivia (Santa Cruz, Uyuni, or La Paz) and explores an island shaped like their department. An automatic 20-second prologue transforms the island tile by tile into a Martian base.

Missions by Sol:

* Sol 1 (Water and plants): Produce water and grow crops by regulating hydrogen and light without depleting air or battery.
* Sol 8 (Storm): Survive a storm by choosing critical systems or cleaning panels while risking radiation exposure.
* Sol 18 (Signal): Calibrate a historic antenna and activate a shield in response to NASA solar alerts.
* Sol 28 (Rover): Drive a rover across Jezero Crater while balancing battery and heating.

Real science and design: Integrates data from the NASA POWER and NASA DONKI APIs, separating fiction from science. It features an Explorer Mode that pauses the simulation during critical drops so players can fix mistakes without frustration, rewarding progress with badges and a Junior Astronaut diploma.
details:
What does it do or how does it work? It is an educational adventure and survival web game designed for children ages 8 to 13. The player selects a city in Bolivia (Santa Cruz, Salar de Uyuni, or La Paz/El Alto) and explores a floating island shaped like a simplified silhouette of that department. Through an automatic 20-second prologue, a fictional alarm transforms the island tile by tile into a Martian base. Accompanied by a guide robot named Chispa, users solve decision-making minigames to produce water and grow food (Sol 1), ration energy during a dust storm (Sol 8), activate a protective shield against space weather alerts (Sol 18), and drive a six-wheeled rover across Jezero Crater (Sol 28). It includes an Explorer Mode that pauses the simulation during critical resource drops so players can fix mistakes without frustration.

What benefits does it offer? It translates complex aerospace engineering concepts (such as ECLSS life support systems and limited resource management) into a playful, accessible format. It runs directly in the browser with synthesized audio (Web Audio API) and procedural graphics, requiring no heavy installations or user accounts. Additionally, it incorporates automatic backups and preloaded data to ensure continuous operation even if the internet connection drops.

What is the intended impact of the project? To democratize STEM education by bringing space science and scientific outreach to children and youth in Bolivia for free. It is designed to be deployed as an interactive station at the American Space in the CBA of Santa Cruz and as a large-scale educational attraction at cultural events such as La Noche Larga de Museos (The Long Night of Museums).

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Languages and Frameworks: TypeScript, React 19, Next.js 16 (using App Router for static export), and Tailwind CSS alongside custom stylesheets (globals.css, world.css, kids.css).
  • Libraries and Architecture: React Context + useReducer (GameProvider), HTML5 Canvas for isometric and procedural rendering of the world and rover, SVG for maps and visual elements, and Web Audio API for sound effects.
  • APIs and Data: Integration with NASA POWER (historical climate reference data) and NASA DONKI (space weather records), backed by local datasets archived in the repository (public/data/).
  • Quality Assurance: Git, GitHub (isabel88k/SpaceZero), and automated tests using Node/tsx (lib/*.test.ts).

In what sense is your project creative? It implements a local "Mirror Effect" that merges Bolivian geographic identity (islands shaped like departmental silhouettes with regional bonuses) with a sci-fi Martian exploration setting. It turns scientific survival scenarios into short-session gamified missions guided by an endearing character (Chispa), and integrates interactive buttons ([?] Real NASA Fact) that clearly separate narrative fiction from actual scientific research.

What factors did your team take into account? Accessibility and inclusion were prioritized with flexible controls (keyboard, click, and touch), support for reduced motion preferences (preventing screen shakes during the prologue for sensitive users), and a mobile-friendly responsive design. Technical robustness was ensured using network cancellation controllers (AbortController), an automatic fallback system with real historical values if APIs fail, over 60 automated tests, and an ethical approach where the final diploma is presented as an internal educational recognition from the game, avoiding any misunderstandings regarding official NASA accreditations.

Source code: https://github.com/isabel88k/SpaceZero
